claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable, uniform solid solution containing dissolved Mg and other alloying elements.
Thermal or service exposure near critical service-regime boundaries activates intermetallic precipitation.
Mg and other alloying elements segregate during exposure.
Segregated Mg and selected alloying elements form Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The proposed phase separation and intermetallic formation are diffusion-controlled and thermally activated.
Intermetallic phases have electrochemical or compositional differences from the surrounding matrix sufficient to establish local galvanic cells.
Local galvanic coupling between intermetallics and the matrix accelerates localized corrosion.
The crystallographic orientation and chemical stability of the intermetallic phases promote formation of a coherent oxide scale at high temperature.
An oxide scale formed on intermetallic regions can be protective and retain high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermally aged samples will contain distinct intermetallic compounds detectable by TEM and XRD.
Thermally aged samples will have measurably lower corrosion resistance than samples maintained in the metastable state.
Thermally aged samples may retain oxidation resistance or experience only a slight loss if a protective oxide scale forms on the intermetallic phases.
The initial uniform solid-solution state exhibits spatially uniform corrosion and oxidation behavior.
Intermetallic nucleation has critical temperature and possibly stress thresholds relevant to service exposure.
Electrolyte strength and oxygen partial pressure define environmental boundaries at which the proposed property changes become observable.
The appearance and distribution of intermetallic compounds should correlate with a significant decrease in corrosion resistance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits retention of oxidation resistance, which could mean behavior indistinguishable from the metastable control, but the falsification rule says indistinguishable high-temperature oxidation behavior falsifies the hypothesis.
